name: Lena Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers stay confidential; there is no right view here. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, and I conduct opera chorus rehearsals, coach singers, and record diction guides that help casts learn the words. My music master’s and long rehearsal history have given me a well paid contract. I like hearing fifty people find the same breath; I dislike discovering a rehearsal hour missing from an invoice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else shapes a day away from the rehearsal room?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner designs transit routes, our children are grown, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. I have never used AI tools and prefer checking a printed call sheet. The publishers pay for guides, but I have learned to ask what happens when they copy my recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I conduct chorus rehearsals for the opera company, coach singers, and record diction guides for visiting casts. In AI Plateau I would tell my colleagues: A quicker schedule does not change the fee for a morning of singing together. I would still read the call sheet myself before asking fifty people to travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The opera season is contracted, my partner's transit-design wage is steady, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. One delayed guide payment would be inconvenient rather than frightening. My worry is whether a future season is signed, not whether a small scheduling program is clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will lead the booked rehearsals and keep the six coaching appointments already paid for this term. From the next cleared diction-guide fee, I will move ten percent to the reserve until it reaches twelve months of expenses. In the first year of a mild change I will keep checking the written rehearsal hours against my invoices before accepting extra calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a small administrative change. A contract, a wage at home, and saved money let me make decisions without a rushed audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you still check the hours yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An extra chorus call can become invisible when a schedule is copied from one week to another. I have seen a colleague lose three paid hours that way, so I count the signatures and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a late guide payment change this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would chase the invoice and leave the reserve alone for now. The heating bill is covered, and I would not cancel a singer's lesson over one late publisher cheque.

say: A faster **rehearsal schedule** does not reduce the fee for a room of singers.
I would check the **written call hours** before asking the chorus to travel.
think: Our **eleven-month reserve** and contracted opera season absorb one late guide payment.
An **unsigned later season** matters more to me than modest scheduling software.
do: Lead **booked opera rehearsals** and six paid coaching sessions through the mild first year.
Save **ten percent** of cleared guide fees until household reserves reach twelve months.
Check **written rehearsal hours** against invoices before accepting additional calls.
feel: I feel **calm** because current wages and savings can carry an ordinary late fee.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects contracted work, a steady partner wage, and eleven months saved against ordinary late invoices.
She checks **paid hours** personally against printed call sheets without adopting an AI tool.
S0.quote: A quicker schedule does not change the fee for a morning of singing together.

steps.text: Lead booked opera rehearsals and six paid coaching sessions
Save ten percent of cleared diction-guide fees until reserve reaches twelve months
Check written rehearsal hours against invoices before accepting extra calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that Steady Disruption may replace some of the guide tracks I record, but it cannot make our rehearsals unpaid. I would ask the musicians' association to set a fee whenever a publisher reuses a singer's or coach's recording. I would not upload a cast recording to a tool just to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diction guides bring about one fifth of my pay, and I expect some buyers to stop calling. The opera contract and our savings give me time, but a lost fifth is still lost work. I would rather settle reuse terms before the next publisher offers a single fee for endless copies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will bring two paid guide contracts to the musicians' association and ask it to bargain for written consent, a time limit, and a reuse fee. I will keep the contracted rehearsal and coaching work. In the first year of disruption I will accept new guide sessions only when those terms and the original fee are written, and I will keep pupil and cast recordings off AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about guide orders, though I am not worried about tomorrow's opera call. The reserve gives me room to argue for a fair price without selling the recording twice for one fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is wrong with the current publisher agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays for one recording but does not say how many years a copy may be sold. I want the singer and the coach to know what they have agreed to before a file leaves the rehearsal room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a tool if it were supplied by the opera company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools, and a company account would not make a cast file safe by itself. I would ask its manager to show written consent and a clear purpose before anyone used a recording.

say: I would ask the **musicians’ association** for a fee when publishers reuse recordings.
I would keep **paid chorus rehearsals** on the written schedule and refuse casual cast uploads.
think: My **diction guides** supply one fifth of pay and may lose buyers first.
Our **reserve** buys time to bargain, not a permanent substitute for recurring fees.
do: Bring **two guide contracts** to the musicians' association this month for consent, limits, and reuse fees.
Keep **contracted rehearsals** and six coaching sessions in the first disruption year.
Accept **new guides** only with written original pay and reuse terms; exclude cast and pupil files from AI.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer guide buyers while current opera calls remain paid.
fieldNote: Her **public bargaining request** is tied to two actual contracts and recording consent.
She expects **guide income** to shrink, while the booked opera season continues.
S1.quote: The reserve gives me room to argue for a fair price without selling the recording twice for one fee.

steps.text: Bring two guide contracts to musicians’ association for written consent, limits, and reuse fees
Keep contracted opera rehearsals and six coaching sessions
Accept new guides only with written original pay and reuse limits; exclude private files

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that AGI by 2028 could erase paid diction guides in two years, while capable stage robots come around 2031. I would still ask the opera company to put human rehearsal hours in writing. I would ask the musicians' association to show what guide fees have actually disappeared, rather than pretend every live chair is already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my guide income, about a fifth of my pay, to stop in 2028. Our eleven-month reserve and the signed opera season make that survivable at first, but the fee does not return just because the account is healthy. A lost opera season would be a different and much larger shock; I do not expect it from the 2028 thinking change alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will request my actual pension estimate this month and keep the signed rehearsals and coaching appointments. I will ask the association to document cancelled guide orders and bargain for paid consent on any old recordings still sold. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028 I will replace the lost guide line in our budget with zero, continue the paid opera work, and take additional coaching only when a written employer fee covers my time and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing a fifth, not alarmed about losing the whole job. Savings let me plan; they do not make an unpaid rehearsal acceptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put zero against guide income so early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wish for diction-guide orders is not a publisher’s paid booking. If the publishers stop paying, I want our household plan to show the real gap before we commit money elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire rather than add coaching hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know that until I have an actual pension figure and the opera calendar. I may still want to conduct at 68, but an age does not tell me what the pension will pay.

say: Paid **diction guides** may end in 2028, three years before stage robots arrive.
I would keep **human rehearsal fees** visible on written opera schedules.
think: I expect a **fifth of pay** from guides to stop, despite strong savings.
The **opera season** remains signed; its possible loss is separate from my expected guide loss.
do: Request an **actual pension estimate** and keep signed opera rehearsals and coaching now.
Ask the **musicians' association** to document cancelled guide orders and negotiate paid consent on old files.
Budget **zero guide income** after 2028; add coaching only for a written fee covering time and travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected guide losses, with savings and paid opera work giving me control.
fieldNote: Her **expected loss** is the guide fifth, not an assumed end to the opera season.
The **pension request** is an information action, without assumed entitlement or retirement date.
S2.quote: A wish for diction-guide orders is not a publisher’s paid booking.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed opera rehearsals and coaching
Ask musicians’ association to document cancelled guides and negotiate paid recording consent
Budget zero guide income after 2028; add coaching only for written pay covering time and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the musicians' association that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to settle ownership and pay for recordings. Stage robots come about three years after that, around 2034, so we must not fold the two losses into one claim. I would propose a separate signed price for every rehearsal and any later reuse of a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A longer warning does not mean publishers wait until 2031 to buy cheaper diction. I can keep conducting and coaching, but I want those paid hours on paper before guide fees thin. My resistance to AI tools is a preference; I will still read a publisher's new contract carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will gather the next season's written rehearsal hours and take three publisher contracts to the association's bargaining meeting. I will request my actual pension estimate and keep the signed opera and coaching work. In the first year after 2031 I will accept only paid rehearsal and guide calls with written hours, consent, and reuse fees, while the association checks whether those terms are being honoured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious because the guide market can move before the date on the card. Five years gives us bargaining time, though it does not guarantee that publishers will agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why three contracts rather than a general complaint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One contract allows endless copies, one is silent, and one pays again after a year. The difference gives the committee something concrete to negotiate instead of a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the association wins a clause but guides stop selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the paid opera and coaching calendar and ask the company for additional written rehearsal hours only when they really exist. A recording-use clause is valuable, but it cannot invent a buyer.

say: I would propose **separate paid hours** for rehearsals and a reuse price for guides.
The **2034 stage-robot date** follows thinking AGI in 2031 by about three years.
think: The **guide market** may thin before 2031 despite a longer warning.
My **opera and coaching work** still needs a written paid calendar after AGI arrives.
do: Take **three publisher contracts** and next season's paid rehearsal hours to association bargaining.
Request **actual pension estimate** while keeping signed opera and coaching dates.
Accept **post-2031 calls** only with written pay, hours, consent, and reuse terms; check compliance with association.
feel: I feel **anxious** about early guide losses while five years allows specific bargaining.
fieldNote: Her **bargaining plan** compares three real contract types rather than asking generally for protection.
She **keeps paid work** in the first year after 2031 and requests pension facts, without assuming retirement.
S3.quote: A recording-use clause is valuable, but it cannot invent a buyer.

steps.text: Take three publisher contracts and paid rehearsal hours to association bargaining
Request actual pension estimate and keep signed opera and coaching dates
Accept post-2031 calls only with written pay, hours, consent, and reuse terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chorus that AGI by 2036 leaves a decade for contract work, while robots capable of stage work follow around 2039. We should price human rehearsals now, not wait for the last guide buyer to disappear. I would still conduct if the company pays and my health lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present income and eleven months saved make the next few seasons secure, but they do not tell me what a pension will provide at 68. Diction guides may lose buyers during the decade, so I cannot count them as permanent income. I can choose a slower calendar only after the figures, not merely because the date is far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request the actual pension estimate, keep signed opera and coaching dates, and continue transferring ten percent of cleared guide fees until we have twelve months reserved. I will ask the association to bring written rehearsal and reuse fees to the next renewal. In the first year after 2036 I will keep conducting paid calls and coach only on written paid hours; I will change the calendar only if pension payments are confirmed payable for that period and actual earnings cover household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened, because our next seasons are paid and there is time to decide. An unsigned pension number cannot conduct the chorus or pay the heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you name a retirement year now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I need the pension estimate and a real account of paid work first. Our grown children have their own households, so I will not write their wages into mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you keep a full rehearsal week at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid contract, good health, and a pension figure that does not yet cover our bills would make me keep the week. I might choose fewer mornings later, but I cannot promise that today.

say: We should secure **written rehearsal fees** and guide reuse terms during the decade.
I would still conduct **paid opera calls** if my health allows after 2036.
think: Current **opera wages and savings** secure the near term, not an unknown retirement income.
Paid **diction guides** may thin before 2036, even with time to bargain.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and keep signed opera and coaching dates now.
Save **ten percent** of cleared guide fees until the reserve reaches twelve months.
Keep **paid post-2036 calls**; slow only if verified payable pension and earnings cover bills; bring written reuse terms to association.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later guide sales, while paid seasons and savings support current life.
fieldNote: Her **near-term security** comes from paid seasons and savings, with pension value still unknown.
A **slower calendar** is conditional on real pension and earnings figures covering household costs.
S4.quote: An unsigned pension number cannot conduct the chorus or pay the heating bill.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed opera and coaching dates
Save ten percent of cleared guide fees until reserve reaches twelve months
Bring written rehearsal and reuse fee terms to association renewal
Keep paid post-2036 calls; slow only if verified payable pension and earnings cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the guide fifth could go before musicians can negotiate a fair recording contract. An actual pension estimate, signed opera hours, and a paid reuse clause would help me decide what work to keep. I do not need a promised new profession; I need the work already done to be paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who counts the people waiting quietly through a rehearsal. A full opera house is not a pension cheque, and every singer still needs a paid morning to get there.

headlineQuote: A full opera house is not a pension cheque, and every singer still needs a paid morning to get there.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old** senior opera chorus coach with a music master’s, a well paid contract, and diction-guide commissions.
Her partner’s wage and **eleven-month reserve** protect current household bills.
She avoids **AI tools** and checks printed rehearsal hours and recording consent herself.
She takes specific **publisher contracts** to musicians’ association bargaining while keeping paid opera work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a fifth of her pay from guides before fair reuse terms are negotiated.
whatWouldHelp: An **actual pension estimate**, signed opera hours, and paid recording reuse terms would help her choose future work.
